abstract: Abstract Introduction: Alveolar Capillary Dysplasia (ACD) and Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD) are grave conditions affecting primarily the lung at different developmental stages. Endothelial Cell (EC) involvement is paramount to their progression. FOXF1-expressing endothelial cells (FOXF1+ ECs) are a subpopulation of the pulmonary endothelium that have significant angiogenic and vasculogenic potential. Absence of FOXF1+ECs has been linked to ACD and these cells are found in decreased numbers in BPD. Transplantation of these cells has great therapeutic potential and ameliorates the phenotypes in mouse models of ACD and BPD. However, these cells have limited bioavailability and the identification of other sources is warranted. Here, we investigate the presence of FOXF1+ ECs in the placental tissues. Methods: Human and Murine placentas were investigated via immunohistochemistry (IF), flow cytometry (FC) for the presence and characterization of FOXF1+ ECs. Comparative transcriptomic analyses performed between the EC component of mouse placentas and lungs. Subsequently, engraftment assay of murine placental FOXF1+ ECs was performed in a mouse model of ACD. Results: Human FOXF1+ ECs were identified in the chorion and umbilical cord. Similarly to human placentas, the presence of placental FOXF1+ ECs via IHC and FC was observed in murine placentas of different developmental stages. Transcriptomic expression analyses revealed three distinct murine placental endothelial populations, one of which co-expresses FOXF1 and stem cell factor (Kit). This population was found to have similar transcriptional signature to the pulmonary counterparts. Next, placentally derived FOXF1+ ECs from transgenic mice (expressing GFP-reporter knocked into the endogenous FOXF1 gene locus) were transplanted into a mouse model of ACD where engraftment was documented. Discussion: FOXF1+ ECs have been previously described only in the pulmonary vasculature. With this study, we describe the existence of a population in placental tissues. This population has significant phenotypic expression overlap with their pulmonary counterparts and is able to engraftment into the pulmonary vasculature. These attributes are important not only from a developmental perspective but also from a potential therapeutic standpoint as placentas can act as a cell harvesting pool for these cells. Placental tissues are commonly discarded despite harboring a plethora of stem cells where their utilization especially in cases of auto transplantation to at-risk populations like extreme preterm babies are of potential benefit.

abstract: Abstract Introduction: Mechanotransduction in the lung plays a role in fibrogenesis, however the direct role of mechanical changes on microvascular endothelial cells (EC) in the context of pulmonary fibrosis is not well defined. EC sense injury through exposure to circulating mediators and changes in their physical environment, including stiffness. Many injuries cause transient mechanical alterations, but aberrant or sustained mechanical activation may lead to persistently altered endothelial cell states as seen in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Rho kinase (ROCK), a well-documented mechanosensor, regulates EC barrier function, inflammatory and pro-fibrotic signaling. We and others have shown that persistent, sustained vascular leak exacerbates injury-induced pulmonary fibrosis regardless of injury. We hypothesize that EC ROCK inhibition will block early mechanotransduction events key to initiating a feedback loop of permeability and pro-fibrotic signaling, to preventing progressive fibrosis in IPF. Methods: For this study we utilized publicly available scRNAseq data sets of lung tissue collected from IPF and control subjects. Established pre-clinical models of bleomycin induced pulmonary fibrosis (single and repetitive dosing) were used to test the ability of genetic ROCK deletion to attenuate mortality and lung fibrosis (Hydroxyproline Assay, Ashcroft Scoring) after injury. Human lung microvascular endothelial cells and normal human lung fibroblasts were used in in vitro systems with commercially available hydrogels (1-25kPa) to further investigate the role of mechanical induction of endothelial ROCK-dependent signaling to promote EC cell state changes (ACKR1, IGFBP7, COL15) and paracrine fibroblast activation (CTHRC1, COL1A1 and POSTN). Results: Public scRNAseq datasets were interrogated for differential expression. Within a fibrosis associated EC cluster (COL15+, ACKR1+, IGFBP7+), we found increased expression of ROCK isoforms, as well as upregulation of mechanotransduction associated genes. Inducible EC specific ROCK2 deletion was protective in both a single dose and repetitive dosing model of bleomycin induced lung fibrosis. In vitro, we observed increased ROCK activity (p-cofilin) as well as markers of fibrosis associated endothelial cells with ECM stiffness that was inhibited with pharmacologic ROCK inhibition. Normal human lung fibroblasts (nHLFb) cultured on physiologic stiffness (1kPa) became activated upon exposure to conditioned media from stiffness activated EC. Conclusions: We find that lung ECs from IPF patients are highly mechanically activated, have increased ROCK activity, and that EC-specific ROCK2 isoform deletion is protective in bleomycin models of lung fibrosis. Our data position EC ROCK signaling at the center of a pathogenic feedforward loop of persistent endothelial barrier dysfunction that perpetuates fibroblast activation to drive the progression of IPF.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Although guidelines recommend the use of provocative testing to diagnose pulmonary venous hypertension (PVH) that is unapparent at normal resting right heart catheterization (RHC), the incremental value of provocative testing is unknown. We aim to evaluate the incremental diagnostic capability of inhaled nitric oxide (iNO), fluid challenge (FC) or invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (iCPET) to unmask PVH using previously defined hemodynamic cutoffs. Methods: We included subjects from the NHLBI-funded Pulmonary Vascular Disease Phenomics (PVDOMICS) study. Our analysis included patients with World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) Group 2 disease (G2PH) and G2PH comparators (WSPH Group 2 phenotype without a diagnosis of PH) as determined by the PI or adjudication panel. We then applied a protocol-driven provocative approach based on the feasibility of modalities available in most catheterization labs. Using a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) cutoff of >15, frequencies were identified for subjects based on resting PCWP and with iNO. Frequencies were also identified for: those who received FC with a PCWP cutoff of ≥18 or those who received iCPET with PCWP cutoff of >20 (upright) or >25 (supine). Results: There were 419 subjects identified with WSPH Group 2 disease (Figure). Roughly half were found to have a PCWP >15 during resting RHC (N = 207). Of the remaining subjects with a resting PCWP ≤15 (N = 150), 42 subjects were found to have a PCWP >15 with iNO administration (40.0%). Of the remaining 63 subjects with PCWP ≤15 following iNO administration, nearly half (N = 26, 48.0%) demonstrated a PCWP ≥18 following FC while 8 subjects (14.8%) demonstrated an elevated PCWP following iCPET. Conclusions: There is a high proportion of G2PH patients (∼35%) who appear hemodynamically similar to precapillary PH at rest. Inhaled nitric oxide vasodilatory challenge unmasks G2PH in many patients. In situations where iNO does not disclose the G2PH phenotype, provocation with FC or iCPET can be useful as a supplementary provocative maneuver. Future directions will focus on agnostically assessing the utility of provocation based on grouping subjects by resting hemodynamics as well as assessing the use of provocation in other forms of PH.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) is a progressive and debilitating disease for patients and a high burden on caregivers. The comprehensive impact of PAH on health-related quality of life (HRQoL), economic stability, and the downstream societal burden remains poorly understood. We described the impact of PAH on work productivity, daily activities, HRQoL, and caregiving in the United States (US). Methods: Between September-October 2024 a prospective, cross-sectional survey was fielded in a nationally representative sample of patients from a US rare disease panel aged ≥18 years with self-reported PAH diagnosis (World Health Organization Group 1 PH), right heart catheterization, and at least one PAH-targeted therapy. The scientific questionnaire included: EQ-5D index score, EQ-5D Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) scale, and customized survey items to assess treatment burden and caregiver support needs. The study was IRB exempt. Analyses were descriptive. Results: As of this 7 October interim analysis, 155 respondents completed the survey (mean age=51.6; female=93.5%, White=80%). Most reported functional class II (45.2%) or III (40.6%). The proportions who reported mono, dual, triple, or more than 3 therapies were 13.5%, 31.0%, 41.3%, and 14.2%, respectively. Scores (mean ± standard deviation) for EQ-5D were 0.63 ± 0.22 [scale: 0=dead to 1=full health] and for EQ-5D VAS were 63.1 ± 17.5 [scale: 0=worst to 100=best], indicating substantial impact on quality of life. PAH affected respondents’ ability to work, with 41.3% changing from full- to part-time employment and 49.0% decreasing their work hours. Among those currently employed (29.7%), in the past 7-days 17.2% ± 26.7 missed work and 36.7% ± 22.3 reported suboptimal functioning while at work. Nearly all (n=133, 85.8%) respondents had a caregiver to help with daily activities. Among those with at least one caregiver the most common caregivers were unpaid: partner/spouse (76%), followed by children (59%), and friend/neighbor (53%). Caregivers frequently missed work to assist patients with daily activities. Proportionally, partners/spouses missed work the most (59.4%), followed by other family members (32.3%), and children (28.2%). For patients with paid caregivers (n=15, 9.7%), out-of-pocket costs per month ranged from $0 to $100. Results will be presented by functional class. Conclusions: PAH detracts from both patient and caregiver quality of life, decreasing daily functional capacity and economic productivity. Early findings quantify this burden and underscore the potential importance of programs to alleviate both the medical and socioeconomic burden of PAH on patients and their families.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Survivors of tuberculosis (TB) experience an increased risk of mortality following TB treatment as compared to the general population. To better understand the wide spectrum of post-TB disease and differences in outcomes, we sought to identify clinical phenotypes among individuals with a history of TB who were admitted to a tertiary care hospital. Methods: A k-prototype cluster analysis was performed using data from a case-control study of adults admitted to Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital in Eldoret, Kenya between 2019 and 2022. The original case-control study focused on chronic hypoxemia and found that prior TB was an important risk factor for chronic hypoxemia in the population. Twenty-one variables, of a possible 78, were chosen based on data completeness, clinical relevance, and for chest x-ray data, inter-reader reliability. Silhouette index was assessed to determine the optimal number of clusters among participants with a history of prior TB. Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests were used to compare differences in characteristics and mortality outcomes between clusters and participants with no TB history. Results: The dataset included 417 participants, of whom 58 (12.8%) had a history of prior TB. Two distinct prior TB clusters were identified (Table 1). Cluster 1 (n=29) is characterized by younger, predominantly female individuals with no smoking history and a high rate of HIV infection. Cluster 2 (n=29) is characterized by older, predominantly male individuals with high rates of tobacco use and higher rates of pleural abnormalities and pneumothorax on chest x-ray. Cluster 2 participants had higher St. George's Respiratory Questionnaire symptom scores than Cluster 1; total, activity, and impact scores were similar between clusters. Combined inpatient and 1-month post discharge mortality was 31% for Cluster 1 and 24% for Cluster 2. Conclusions: Distinct clinical phenotypes among individuals with prior TB were identified using routinely available demographic, clinical, and imaging data. These phenotypes inform outcomes and can potentially be used to tailor interventions to improve diagnosis and treatment of post-TB complications among TB survivors in high-TB burden settings. Future research should explore clinical phenotypes in a prospectively enrolled cohort of individuals who are treated for TB and followed post treatment in order to validate findings.

abstract: Abstract RATIONALE: Patient isolation has been widely utilized to reduce in hospital transmission of infectious and multidrug resistant pathogens. While necessary in certain cases, patient isolation is associated with decreased frequency and duration of nursing and physician interactions and higher rates of preventable adverse events including falls, ulcers, and electrolyte abnormalities. Despite these negative patient safety outcomes little is known about the effects of patient isolation on rates of clinical deterioration and in hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). We sought to determine the association of patient isolation on in hospital cardiac arrest. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective review of a prospectively collected database of in hospital cardiac arrest at a single large academic medical center in the US. In this institution a biweekly multidisciplinary review of all IHCA is conducted to assign primary and secondary drivers to each case. Commonly assigned drivers include delayed diagnosis, inappropriate level of care, related to underlying diagnoses, failure of palliation, and treatment concerns. We reviewed all patients in this registry with IHCA occurring outside of the ICU with a primary driver of delayed diagnosis. Primary analysis looked at the presence of isolation orders during the index hospitalization as well as the indication for and type of isolation. RESULTS: A total of 53 cases of IHCA occurred outside of the ICU with a primary driver of delayed diagnosis. Within this group 29 patients (55%) had orders for isolation during their hospitalization. The greatest number of IHCA occurred in those on enhanced precautions, 36%, and those on contact precautions for Clostridium difficile, 35%, representing more than half of IHCA in patients requiring isolation precautions. CONCLUSIONS: We found a substantial proportion of patients with IHCA occurring outside of the ICU due to delays in diagnosis had an order for isolation during their hospitalization. As a result of this a multidisciplinary team was created to investigate the potential association of isolation precautions with IHCA with ongoing PDSA cycles.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Aging leads to changes in gene expression, including increased expression of inflammatory, DNA damage, and innate immunity genes, and decreased expression of wound healing and lipid metabolism genes. Further, some transcriptomic age-related changes are adaptive while others are maladaptive. Overall, aging of the lungs is associated with declining respiratory and immunologic function and increased development and progression of disease. While cigarette smoking is known to accelerate lung aging, it is unknown whether newer tobacco products, such as e-cigarettes, promote lung aging. Here we sought to define effects of vaping on the lung transcriptome related to aging and associated biological pathways. Because our previous work identified numerous gene expression, protein level, and cellular changes in the lungs due to e-cigarette use, we hypothesized that long term exposure to e-cigarettes would cause accelerated lung aging in mice. Methods: Male and female C57BL/6, 6-8 week-old mice were exposed to e-cigarette aerosols (70:30 propylene glycol/glycerol (PG/Gly) + 59mg/mL nicotinic salts (E-cig), 70:30 PG/Gly (Vehicle), Mango- or Mint-flavored JUUL) or room air (control) through a whole-body exposure system (inExpose; SciReq) for 1 hour/day, 5 days/week, for 3 months. Pulmonary arteries were flushed with PBS, lungs were harvested, RNA isolated and RNAseq conducted. An unbiased differential gene expression analysis was performed by comparing each group to air controls within their respective sex groups. Aged-related genes were then selected for biological pathway analysis to identify significantly enriched pathways. Results: E-cigarette and no nicotine (vehicle) aerosol exposures induced similar changes in age-related gene expression in the lung. We identified sex differences, with female mice exhibiting fewer age-related gene expression changes compared to males. Most aging signatures in the flavored e-cigarette exposed mice (Mint and Mango) were expressed in the opposite direction observed with aging, with most genes being downregulated. The antigen processing and presentation and actin cytoskeleton pathways were enriched with genes such as CTSS and ITGAX in male e-cigarette, male vehicle, and female flavored e-cigarette cohorts. The leukocyte transendothelial migration pathway was enriched with genes such as CYBB in both the female flavored and male e-cigarette cohorts. Conclusions: These data demonstrate that chronic inhalation of e-cigarettes aerosols may accelerate lung aging, in a sex-dependent manner. PG and Gly are the primary chemicals within e-cigarette vapor driving gene dysregulation. However, flavorant chemicals may also have harmful effects on age-protective genes. More work is needed to define the underlying mechanisms by which e-cigarettes accelerate lung aging.

abstract: Abstract Purpose: This quality improvement (QI) study evaluates the accuracy of resident attention to tobacco abuse-related health concerns and the provision of appropriate education and treatment to smokers during hospital admission and discharge. Methods: We conducted a retrospective chart review of 390 inpatient admissions over a 2-month period. The study focused on whether smoking status was addressed at the time of discharge, and if appropriate smoking cessation education and treatment were provided to identified smokers. The primary endpoint was to assess whether smoking cessation education/treatment was provided at discharge. The secondary endpoint was to determine if the presence of pulmonary disease influenced attention to smoking status and the offering of education/treatment. Results: Of the 390 charts reviewed, 208 patients were female, 182 were male.231 patients identified as African American, 131 as White, with others identifying as Asian, Hispanic, or Middle Eastern.126 patients were current smokers, 22 were former smokers, and 234 denied any history of tobacco use.81 patients (32.6%) with a history of tobacco use had updated pack-year (PY) documentation. Among these, 35% had 0.1-5 PY, 20% had 10.1-15 PY, and smaller percentages had higher Pack year ranges.Only 0.86% of smokers were prescribed smoking cessation medications.76% of at-risk patients received smoking cessation education, mostly through verbal counseling and instructions.26% of at-risk patients were prescribed cessation medications, with nicotine patches being the most common, and minimal use of other medications (e.g., nicotine gum, Chantix).Among those receiving cessation education, 11% were admitted for COPD exacerbation, 9% for influenza pneumonia, and 7% for conditions like CAP, acute hypoxia, respiratory failure, and cellulitis. Conclusion: While 248 patients had a documented history of tobacco use, only 32.6% had updated pack-year documentation. Smoking cessation education was provided to 76% of at-risk patients, but only 26% received prescriptions for cessation medications, predominantly nicotine patches. Most patients receiving cessation education were admitted for lung-related diseases. The study highlights gaps in smoking history documentation and suboptimal utilization of cessation resources. A standardized protocol for documenting smoking status and prescribing cessation treatments, irrespective of diagnosis, would streamline the process and improve patient care.

abstract: Abstract RATIONALE: Workers vary considerably in basic and health literacy, motivation, information needs, preferred communication modality, and several other factors. Despite this heterogeneity, most occupational health worker communications are still disseminated as “one-size-fits-all”. We apply the underlying logic of precision medicine to information delivery, demonstrating the potential of widely available AI methods to personalize health information, and demonstrates the potential of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models to adjust communications to workers’ individual needs. METHODS: Occupational health (OH) messages from public health and professional society agencies were selected for analysis. Each was automatically customized for worker-specific characteristics and needs (Table 1) using ChatGPT with customized prompts to deliver text and DALL-E 3 (by OpenAI) through the Chat-GPT platformto create images. We are developing automated processes to assess information integrity or loss (e.g., by comparing source and personalized messages using BLEU or ROUGE metrics). RESULTS: Text sources in several categories were identified for evaluation – 1) “Lay person” targeted individual workers; 2) “General clinician” focused on communication for primary clinicians; 3) Technical texts were processed to make the information meaningful to workers and non-OH professionals. Sources included: 1) Agencies such as OSHA, NIOSH, health department; 2) Published abstract or technical report; 3) “Patient education” materials such as from ATS; 4) news articles. Prompts create outputs from source text optimized for patient/worker characteristics (such as limited literacy, age group) and purpose (e.g. “motivate for action”, “get attention”, “explain”.) Image prompts include “cartoon”, “get attention”, “little reading ability”. Prompts are easily generated by user rather than from a prespecified list. Output varies in degree of information loss and text characteristics but > 80% received acceptable-good ratings by domain expert for on-target focus and content. Examples are in figure. CONCLUSION With new GenAI, it will be possible to automated messaging that is highly targeted to optimize effectiveness for specific workers. Evaluation methods including human and machine based are needed to choose optimal and accurate approaches.

abstract: Abstract Lung cancer remains the most prevalent cancer in the United States, with lung adenocarcinoma (a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer) accounting for approximately 40% of cases. Despite advancements in detection and treatment, the prognosis remains poor, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 15%. Lepidic adenocarcinoma, characterized by tumor cell proliferation along intact alveolar walls, can present as nonspecific micronodules and ground-glass opacities on imaging, complicating diagnosis. We report a 72-year-old female with a history of morbid obesity, hypertension, and osteoporosis who presented with progressive shortness of breath. Initial CT imaging revealed diffuse mosaicism and ground-glass opacities with pulmonary micronodules. Extensive workup for infectious and non-infectious etiologies lead to a diagnosis of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) based on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Despite treatment, her symptoms worsened, and a subsequent biopsy revealed lepidic adenocarcinoma. This case highlights the atypical presentation of lepidic adenocarcinoma, often mimicking infectious processes such as PJP. The presence of ground-glass opacities can lead to misdiagnosis due to their non-specific nature, which overlaps with various lung pathologies. The initial PJP diagnosis in an immunocompetent patient raises concerns for an undiagnosed malignancy, emphasizing the need for thorough investigations when encountering unusual pathogens in seemingly healthy individuals. This case underscores the limitations of imaging in distinguishing between various pulmonary pathologies. Despite advancements in imaging, non-specific findings can hinder early detection of malignancies like lepidic adenocarcinoma. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for underlying neoplasms in atypical presentations, particularly when initial diagnoses do not align with clinical progression. This case serves as a reminder of the complexities involved in diagnosing lung cancer amidst overlapping clinical presentations.

abstract: Abstract Introduction and Background Pulmonary fibrosis is originated as a result of dysregulated lung repair and is characterized by excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix and abnormal myofibroblast activation. Multiple cell types are involved in the pathogenesis of fibrosis. Pericytes are becoming an increasingly attractive cell type due to their ability to transition into myofibroblasts under certain stimuli. Transcription factors that regulate this transition are unknown. The goal of this study is to determine whether FOXF1 transcription factor is important for the disease progression. Methods/Approach Transgenic mice were used to conditionally delete or overexpress Foxf1 specifically in pericytes. Bleomycin was used to induce pulmonary fibrosis. H&E/Trichrome/Sirus RED staining, immunofluorescence staining, Hydroxyproline assay, flow cytometry, flow sorting, real time PCR, single cell sequencing were performed to study the role of Foxf1 in pericytes. Flexivent was used to assess lung function during fibrosis. Results We have demonstrated that mRNA and protein levels of FOXF1 are decreased in pericytes within fibrotic regions of human IPF lungs and mouse lungs. Genetic deletion of Foxf1 in pericytes increased severity of pulmonary fibrosis in mice after bleomycin injury, which is shown by upregulated collagen depositions, as well as decreased lung functions and peripheral blood oxygenation. We have also shown increased pericyte-to-myofibroblast transition and and increased accumulation of myofibroblasts and macrophages compared to control mice. Discussion/Conclusions Deletion of FOXF1 in pericytes increases the severity of pulmonary fibrosis, indicating that FOXF1 in pericytes is important for pathogenesis of lung fibrosis. Further studies are needed to determine the mechanism by which loss of Foxf1 in pericytes leads to severe fibrotic phenotype.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Emphysema is a progressive lung disease with highly heterogeneous patterns of progression driven by complex cellular and molecular mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is critical to developing personalized therapeutic strategies. This study integrates a deep learning prognostic model and spatial transcriptomic profiling to identify key cellular and molecular drivers of emphysema progression. Methods: Emphysema severity was quantified as the percentage of low-attenuation areas below -950 Hounsfield Units (%LAA950) using the Chest Imaging Platform software. A generative local density foundational model was trained to captured changes in lung density over 5 years. Embeddings from the foundational model were used to train a transformer deep learning model to predict lobar lung density evolution based on tissue destruction. To investigate the molecular mechanisms, GeoMX Digital Spatial Profiling (DSP) technology was applied to formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) lung sections, targeting small airways, vessels, and parenchyma. Whole transcriptome data were analyzed using R script packages to uncover differential expression patterns and cell-specific immune signatures. Results: A cohort of 20 emphysema patients (average %LAA950 = 22.46) was stratified into fast and slow progression groups based on predictions from the deep learning model. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct immune signatures characterizing fast progressors. In fast progressors, marginal zone B cells, that support adaptive immunity by presenting antigens to T cells and producing antibodies, were enriched in the parenchyma and airways. Proliferating CD4 and CD8 T cells were also increase in parenchyma.Differential gene expression analysis showed significant enrichment of adaptive immune-related genes in fast progressors. These included HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C, associated with cytotoxic CD8+ T cell activation, and HLA-DQB1 and HLA-DRA, linked to exogenous antigen presentation to CD4+ T cells. Additionally, genes such as B2M, CD74, and HLA-DMA, which support antigen presentation, were also upregulated. These genes also indirectly enhance B cell responses by facilitating helper T cell activation, which is critical for adaptive immunity. Conclusions: This study identifies distinct immune profiles associated with emphysema progression. Fast progressors exhibit heightened adaptive immune activation, characterized by cytotoxic T cells, marginal zone B cells, and robust antigen presentation processes. These findings provide novel insights into emphysema's immunopathology and suggest potential immune-mediated therapeutic targets to manage emphysema progression.

abstract: Abstract Rationale:Extreme summer heat is increasing in the United States (US) with climate projections showing that extreme heat events will become more frequent and intense in coming decades. With a rise in average global temperature, the incidence of heat-related deaths has increased with 1,602 deaths in the US in 2021 and 2,302 in 2023. Despite this increase, little is known about the characteristics of patients presenting with non-exertional heat-related illness and risk factors for mortality. We sought to evaluate the characteristics and mortality of patients with heat stroke presenting to a large multi-center health system in the southwestern US. Methods:Retrospective cohort analysis identified heat stroke patients between 2007-2023 that presented to observation, inpatient, or the emergency department in a multi-center health network in the Southwestern United States. Inclusion criteria were adults > 18 years, ICD 9/10 code (992- and T67-). Comorbidities were identified by ICD 10 code. Multivariable logistic regression model was used to evaluate odds of mortality based on patients’ demographics, comorbidities, and associated conditions. Results:Our cohort included 12,200 patients with heat stroke. Mean age was 48.4 (19.1 SD). and 70.8% were male. The cohort included 62.4% White, 8.0% Black, 23.5% Hispanic, and 3.5% Native American patients. Comorbidities included diabetes 21.7%, hypertension 43.8%, COPD 11.5%, CKD 10.6%, CAD 14.2%, CHF 10.0%, sepsis 15.8%, obesity 14.3%, pneumonia 21.8%, liver failure 14.9%. A smaller percentage of patients had HIV 0.86% and cancer 1.8%. Drug use, methamphetamine use, and alcohol use was reported in 42.6%, 16.9%, and 15.7% of patients, respectively. Overall, the mortality was 1.23% (150/12,200 patients). On multivariable analysis (after controlling for age, sex, race, and comorbid conditions) sepsis (adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 2.80; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.79 – 4.38), pneumonia (aOR 2.01; 95% CI 1.29 – 3.11), ARDS (aOR 4.96, 95% CI 2.14 – 11.48), and liver failure (aOR 3.94, 95% CI 2.61 – 5.95) had the highest odds of mortality. Interestingly, patients with methamphetamine use had a trend towards increased mortality (aOR 1.42, 95% CI 0.93-2.18, p=0.086) though these findings did not reach statistical significance. We did not find differences in mortality by race/ethnic background either. Conclusions:Overall mortality associated with heat stroke was low, 1.23% in this cohort. Patients with heat stroke and sepsis, pneumonia, liver failure, and ARDS experienced the highest risk of mortality.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Determining circulating proteins robustly associated with mortality is an essential step in identifying novel therapeutic targets to test in critically ill COVID-19 patients. Methods: We identified and validated circulating protein levels associated with mortality in critically ill COVID-19 patients using an aptamer-based proteomics platform (Somalogic). We analyzed two prospective cohorts: (1) single-site COVID-19 Host Response and Clinical Outcomes (CHROme) (discovery cohort, N=198) and (2) multi-site Severe Acute Respiratory Infection – Preparedness (SARI-PREP) (validation cohort, N=100). Associations between 4,718 plasma protein levels collected within 48 hours of ICU admission and 14-day mortality were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for age, sex, and BMI (FDR <0.01). We performed over-representation analysis to annotate top protein associations. We cross-referenced our validated protein set with single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in cis-associated genes associated with mortality in the COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative (HGI) GWAS (PMID: 34237774). To further assess whether the validated proteins might be causal intermediates, we analyzed pooled genotype and proteomic data from CHROme and SARI-PREP to determine if identified SNPs were cis-protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs). Results: In the discovery cohort, 1,529 proteins were associated with increased risk, while 71 proteins were associated with reduced risk of 14-day mortality. Validation confirmed that 520 of these proteins were associated with increased risk, and three—BCHE, SERPINC1, and F2—were associated with reduced risk. The top 100 proteins included pro-inflammatory biomarkers (ADM, CCL19, CD46), circulating immune receptors (CD300C, TNFRSF1B), interferon-associated biomarkers (IFNAR1, INHBA/INHBB, IFNGR1), and novel biomarkers related to neuronal development (NLGN2, NLGN1, NLGN4X). Over-representation analysis (reference Hallmark Pathways) revealed enrichment in immune pathways (inflammatory response, IL6-STAT2 signaling and TNF-α via NF-κB signaling) and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Five proteins in the validated set have a cis-SNP that was significantly associated with mortality in the COVID-19 HGI GWAS: CD300C (rs4351086), EPHB4 (rs314296), EPHA7 (rs76462658), PDGFRA (rs1553659), and B3GALT1 (rs78286703). Exploratory causal inference analyses in genotyped subjects from both cohorts (n = 249), did not identify cis pQTLs between these SNPs and protein levels or associations with mortality that met our FDR threshold. However, rs4351086 (CD300C – co-inhibitory receptor on antigen-presenting cells) and rs314296 (EPHB4 –receptor that plays a key role in vascular development) have been previously associated with gene expression (eQTLgen.org). Conclusions: Our analysis identified and validated previously unreported immune mediators and soluble receptors that are associated with mortality in severe COVID-19. Further investigation is required to determine whether these proteins are causal intermediates.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Asthma endotypes may be broadly categorized into high type 2 (T2) asthma and low T2 asthma. Small airway dysfunction (SAD) contributes to the clinical manifestations of asthma. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effect of T2 inflammation and SAD on clinical phenotypes related to asthma severity. Methods: High T2 and low T2 asthma were defined as patients with asthma and blood eosinophil count (BEC) ≥300 and <300 cells/μL, respectively. Clinical high/low SAD clusters were generated in the AssessmenT of smalL Airways involvemeNT In aSthma (ATLANTIS) study (Postma, Lancet Respir Med, 2019). Association analyses of clinical phenotypes and four groups categorized by the combination of high-low T2 asthma and high-low SAD clusters were performed using generalized linear models. Results: Patients with asthma in the ATLANTIS (n = 727) were grouped into HH (high BEC and high SAD; n = 114), HL (high BEC and low SAD; n = 141), LH (low BEC and high SAD; n = 172), and LL (low BEC and low SAD; n = 300). Two high T2 groups had significantly higher fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) levels and sputum % eosinophils than two low T2 groups (HH vs. LH or HL vs. LL; P ≤ 0.0001); two high SAD groups and two low SAD groups were not significantly different for FeNO and sputum % eosinophils (HH vs. HL or LH vs. LL; P > 0.05). Two high SAD groups had significantly higher % predicted R5-20 (resistance of small-to-mid-sized airways), AX (area of reactance), X5 (reactance of more central, conducting small airways at 5 Hz), and a composite ordinal score based on these three impulse oscillometry variables (Kraft, Lancet Respir Med, 2022) than two low SAD groups (P < 0.0001); two high T2 groups and two low T2 groups were not significantly different for these four variables (P > 0.05). Both high T2 inflammation and high SAD scores contributed to lower baseline % predicted FEV1 (HH: 68%; HL: 87%; LH: 71%; LL: 90%), higher % of severe asthma (HH: 70%; HL: 34%; LH: 45%; LL: 34%), and higher % of prospective exacerbations in one year (HH: 36%; HL: 14%; LH: 19%; LL: 12%); in general, high SAD scores showed stronger effect than high T2 inflammation on these variables. Conclusion: T2 inflammation and SAD reflect two independent facets of asthma severity. The combination of high T2 and high SAD leads to more severe asthma endotype.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Inflammation often persists even after smoking cessation, suggesting a self-sustaining pathogenic process similar to autoimmune diseases. However, the specific role of B cells in COPD onset and progression remains underexplored. Methods: We analyzed lung and peripheral blood samples from 61 COPD patients and healthy controls using single-cell transcriptomics to characterize B cell subpopulations and their association with emphysema severity. High emphysema was defined as greater than 5% lobar emphysema and greater than 15% total emphysema. B cell receptor (BCR) sequencing and clonal analysis assessed mutational frequency, clonal expansion, variable gene usage, and CDR3 region diversity. Autoantigen microarrays evaluated autoantibodies in the blood and the lung associated with different clinical characteristics. In contrast, mass spectrometry-based differential antigen capture assays evaluated plasma proteins reactive to lung self-antigens. Analyses were conducted in R, and statistical tests were corrected for multiple-hypothesis testing. Results: Lung B cells were significantly enriched in patients with high emphysema, with quantitative correlations observed between B cell abundance, emphysema severity, and pulmonary function tests (p< 0.05; Figure 1A-D). Within B cell subpopulations, MZ-like cells – defined as highly expressing IGHM and NR4A with enrichment in TNFα-NFκB and STAT3 pathways – were enriched in patients with increased emphysema (p=7.7e-11; Figure 1C-E). Spatial transcriptomics demonstrated these MZ-like cells were increased in lung follicles and airways. Furthermore, immunofluorescence and flow cytometry confirm the presence of this cell type in patients’ lung tissue. B cell receptor sequencing analysis indicated a higher mutational frequency in IGHM isotypes (p=2.9e-6) and shorter CDR3 regions (p=0.0089) among patients with severe emphysema. Clonally expanded cells in patients with emphysema were more common in MZ-like cells (p=2.0e-8), with expanded clones shared in both the lungs and blood (Figure 1F-I). Similar CDR3 motifs were also shared across patients with clonally expanded MZ-like cells. Additionally, patients with high emphysema demonstrated recurrent usage of specific variable genes, including IGHV1-69 and IGHV4-34 (Figure 1J). Autoantigen microarrays revealed that patients with elevated lung MZ-like cell counts also had IGHM-predominant autoantibodies in the lungs and blood (p<0.05; Figure 1K-L). Patients’ sera were also autoreactive to lung IGHM in patients with increased MZ-like cells. Conclusions: This study identifies a novel immune cell population – MZ-like B cells – enriched in severe emphysema. These cells may drive local and systemic autoantibody production, reminiscent of autoimmune diseases. Targeting MZ-like B cells or modulating IGHM autoantibody production presents a promising therapeutic avenue for addressing B cell-mediated mechanisms in COPD.

abstract: Abstract Introduction Diagnosing systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) flares is challenging due to its varied manifestations and its similarity to other rheumatological and inflammatory conditions. SLE flares can be triggered by various factors, including infections, stress, and environmental influences. Prompt diagnosis is essential to initiate treatment and prevent serious consequences. Here, we present a case of an atypical SLE flare presentation. Case Report A 26-year-old male with a complex history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was transferred to a higher level of care. At the previous hospital, he was treated for septic shock due to bacteremia. His hospitalization was further complicated by digital ischemia in all extremities, initially thought to be related to vasopressor use. However, the discovery of a large thrombus in the right atrium extending into the superior vena cava (SVC), along with multiple thrombotic events and a history of SLE, raised a strong suspicion of catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS). Given this suspicion, the patient received pulse-dose steroids and plasmapheresis, and biomarkers were collected before treatment. Surprisingly, antiphospholipid (aPL) antibodies returned negative, with normal C3/C4 levels. ANA and dsDNA antibodies were found at 1:80 and 61.0 IU/mL H, respectively.Additionally, a cavitary pulmonary lesion led to testing for Coccidioides serology, which confirmed coccidioidomycosis IgM positivity. The patient was treated with fluconazole 400 mg daily. Unfortunately, the digital ischemia progressed to dry gangrene, resulting in amputations of the affected extremities. Discussion While clinical suspicion for CAPS was understandable given the patient's complications, the negative antiphospholipid (aPL) antibody levels make this diagnosis unlikely. The normal C3 and C4 levels are also unusual in an SLE flare. Although low C3 and C4 levels are highly specific markers during an SLE flare (93.3% and 82.2%, respectively), their sensitivity is limited (22.6% and 41.9%, respectively)Similarly, dsDNA titers have a specificity of 90% to 99.3% and sensitivity ranging from 38% to 66.8% for SLE flares. Due to the limited sensitivity of these biomarkers, they should ideally be measured together to improve sensitivity for diagnosing this potentially life-threatening condition. In this patient, we suspect that either coccidioidomycosis or a bacterial infection triggered both the SLE flare and the hypercoagulable state. Conclusion The diagnosis of SLE flare is challenging as it has a variable presentation and manifestation. The current available biomarkers have low sensitivity, therefore high clinical index of suspicion is warranted for prompt diagnosis and treatment.

abstract: Abstract Introduction: Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) is a common virus that often remains undiagnosed until symptoms manifest, typically as oral or genital lesions. Neonates are particularly vulnerable, with a high risk of mortality. Neonatal HSV is primarily acquired during vaginal delivery but can also occur in utero or postnatally. It is classified into three main types: infections localized to the skin, eyes, and mouth; central nervous system disease; and disseminated disease (4). Diagnosis typically involves blood and cerebrospinal fluid PCR testing. Despite the risks, routine screening for HSV in pregnant women is not generally recommended, and guidelines vary for prophylaxis treatment (1). This case report discusses a neonate with respiratory failure due to HSV pneumonitis and brings to consideration the current guidelines of HSV infections. Case: A full-term infant, born via vaginal delivery to a mother with a remote history of HSV, exhibited excessive sleepiness at home. Patient was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) due to respiratory distress, requiring bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP). Labs remarkable for elevated procalcitonin, C-reactive protein, and an elevated white blood cell count. A respiratory viral panel was negative, and chest X-ray showed non-focal opacification. Blood and urine cultures were taken, but no lumbar puncture was performed initially. The infant was started on ampicillin-sulbactam and gentamycin for suspected neonatal sepsis. Despite treatment, respiratory failure necessitated intubation. Workup for HSV was initiated, and acyclovir administered. The infant's condition worsened, requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) for hypercarbic hypoxemic respiratory failure. HSV PCR revealed over 13,000 copies/mL, confirming the diagnosis. The infant was decannulated after one week and ultimately discharged on extended oral acyclovir therapy. Discussion: This case underscores the complexity and severity of neonatal HSV infections, which can present without typical skin lesions, as seen in this infant. Current guidelines do not recommend routine HSV screening in pregnancy, which raises questions about whether history-taking should include HSV status to guide prophylactic treatment given high risk of neonatal complications. The standard care for suspected neonatal sepsis includes broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals including acyclovir based on risk factors. Studies however suggest that only 84% of infants receive acyclovir when neonatal sepsis is suspected, despite untreated neonatal HSV having an 80% mortality rate (2)(3). This case highlights the need for heightened awareness and consideration of HSV in neonatal care to improve outcomes. Further research is needed for evaluation of maternal suppressive therapy and association with neonatal HSV.

abstract: Abstract RATIONALE: The lung-brain axis has emerged as a significant area of clinical importance with central nervous system and respiratory system injuries demonstrating bi-directional impact. Unfortunately, effective therapeutics for addressing this pathological cross talk remains an unmet need, due in part to the absence of reliable biomarkers that reflect the severity of lung-brain axis disruption. We assessed specific biomarkers in subjects with traumatic brain injury (TBI), a major public health concern affecting 1.4million Americans annually, and subjects with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), a life-threatening inflammatory lung injury responsible for more than 10% of ICU admissions each year with a 30-40% mortality. METHODS: Serum collected from TBI subjects (n=63, ∼47y/o, ∼20hr post), ARDS (n=39, ∼52y/o, ∼ day 1), and healthy patients (n=40, ∼50y/o) was analyzed via Meso Scale Discovery ELISA for inflammatory biomarkers (eNAMPT, IL-6, PSGL-1, ANG-2, IL-1β, IL-1RA, TNF-α, S100A8) and neurotrauma biomarkers (Glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP], Neuro filament light chain [NFL], Tau). Outliers were removed via ROUT analysis; results were analyzed utilizing Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis w/ Dunn, and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve analysis. RESULTS: All biomarkers were significantly elevated in TBI patients compared to controls except for PSGL-1 (4xeNAMPT, 21x IL-6, 2x Ang-2, 13x IL-1β,3x IL-1RA, 2x TNF-α, 3x S100A8, 136xGFAP, 9x NFL, 9x Tau). ARDS patients demonstrated significantly elevated levels of all biomarkers compared to controls except for GFAP (8x eNAMPT, 12x IL-6, 5xAng-2, 13x IL-1β, 6x IL-1RA, 1.3xPSGL-1, 3x TNF-α, 3x S100A8, 11x NFL, 5xTau). Comparing ARDS to TBI, IL-6 was significantly higher in TBI subjects (2x)whereas eNAMPT, TNF-α, and Ang-2 were all significantly elevated (2x) in ARDS. GFAP was significantly elevated only in TBI. CONCLUSIONS: The elevations in inflammatory biomarkers in TBI- and ARDS-exposed subjects without neuro trauma reflect shared activation of innate immunity consistent with the observation that 25% of TBI patients develop lung injury (including ARDS) supporting lung brain axis disruption. GFAP appears to be a TBI-specific biomarker with the elevations in NFL and Tau in ARDS subjects potentially reflecting peripheral neurological damage without lung brain axis disruption. Longitudinal studies of well-phenotyped TBI and ARDS subjects are needed to disclose the integrated inflammatory responses and the value of inflammatory biomarker testing to detect bidirectional injuries.

abstract: Abstract RATIONALE: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) carries high morbidity and mortality, often compounded by acute kidney injury (AKI) necessitating continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). While lung-protective ventilation is a priority, limited data link these settings to renal outcomes in ARDS, and few studies consider biological factors like age, sex, race, and ethnicity. This study examines how ventilator parameters influence CRRT needs and ARDS outcomes across these biological variables. METHODS: Using a multi-center ARDS cohort dataset, we analyzed associations between baseline ventilator settings—positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), tidal volume (TV), plateau pressure (PPLAT), and driving pressure—and CRRT requirements, as well as ARDS outcomes (ICU-free days, ventilator-free days, and time to death). Logistic and linear regression models, adjusted for age, sex, race, and ethnicity, evaluated the relationships between ventilator parameters, CRRT requirements, and ARDS outcomes. Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed CRRT's impact on mortality, and model coefficients were visualized in a heatmap to illustrate the effects of ventilation parameters on outcomes. RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly reduced survival for CRRT users (p<1e-4). Overall, higher baseline PEEP, PPLAT, and driving pressure were associated with an increased likelihood of requiring CRRT, although this trend was reversed among Hispanic patients. CRRT use was linked to fewer ICU- and ventilator-free days, though this association was not significant for Black, Hispanic, and female patients. Outcome prediction models highlighted further divergent trends across biological variables, particularly for PPLAT settings among females. CONCLUSION: Baseline ventilator settings and CRRT status are significant determinants of clinical outcomes in ARDS patients. High baseline PEEP, PPLAT, and driving pressure correlate with increased CRRT needs and reduced ICU- and ventilator-free days, although these associations vary by age, sex, race, and ethnicity. These findings emphasize the need to integrate these variables into future research and individualized management plans. Tailored respiratory strategies could optimize ARDS outcomes across diverse populations.

abstract: Abstract RATIONALE FREEDOM-EV was a global, event-driven trial demonstrating that oral treprostinil (TRE) delayed disease progression with improvements in WHO FC and NT-proBNP for patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). The 7th World Symposium recommended oral prostacyclins only for intermediate-low risk patients at follow-up. In FREEDOM-EV, 22% of participants were intermediate-high risk at baseline using COMPERA 2.0. We conducted this post-hoc analysis of intermediate-high risk participants in FREEDOM-EV to explore the efficacy and safety of oral TRE in this subgroup. METHODS This analysis only included FREEDOM-EV participants classified as intermediate-high risk by COMPERA 2.0. Time to clinical worsening was compared between oral TRE and placebo (PBO) using Cox regression, reporting hazard ratio (HR), 95% confidence interval (CI), and p-value. COMPERA 2.0 and REVEAL Lite 2 risk scores were assessed from baseline and week 24 (W24) for participants with available 6MWD, WHO FC, and NT-proBNP data. Oral TRE dosing and adverse events were summarized. RESULTS Of the 153 intermediate-high risk participants (77 oral TRE, 76 PBO) in this analysis, clinical worsening occurred in 36% of oral TRE participants and 61% of PBO participants, resulting in a 38% risk reduction (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.38-0.99, p=0.047). Two of the five first-event deaths occurred within the first year for oral TRE versus six of the eight for PBO. Of oral TRE participants (n=59), 46% improved their risk status and 53% maintained by W24, compared to 36% and 62%, respectively, in PBO participants (n=50); one participant worsened in each group. The mean (SD) REVEAL Lite 2 score for oral TRE was 8.7 (1.2) at baseline (n=77) and 7.3 (2.5) at W24 (n=59) versus 8.8 (1.2) (n=76) and 7.9 (1.7) (n=48) for PBO. The median (IQR) oral TRE dose at W24 was 3.8 (2.5, 6.5) mg TID, similar to the overall FREEDOM-EV population (3.6 (2.3, 5.5) mg TID). The safety profile of oral TRE in the intermediate-high population was consistent with the overall FREEDOM-EV population. CONCLUSIONS In this post-hoc analysis of FREEDOM-EV intermediate-high risk participants, oral TRE significantly reduced the risk of clinical worsening and improved or maintained risk profiles in most participants, with a safety profile comparable to the overall FREEDOM-EV population. This suggests that oral TRE can be considered for intermediate-high risk patients with PAH. Further, the EXPEDITE study strategy (rapid parenteral induction and transition to oral treprostinil) may allow more intermediate-high risk patients to benefit from oral TRE. abstract: Abstract RATIONALE: Club cell secretory protein (CC16), an abundantly secreted protein in the airways, plays a crucial role in protecting against respiratory pathogens by promoting secretion of epithelial host-defense factors and limiting infection and inflammation. CC16 levels are reduced in cigarette smokers and further diminished in smokers with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), correlating with disease severity. Murine models of chronic cigarette smoke-induced COPD have shown that CC16 deficiency exacerbates lung inflammation and promotes emphysema development. Further, loss of CC16 expression results in increased susceptibility to infection in vitro and in vivo, highlighting its importance in host defense. While it is commonly known that individuals exposed to cigarette smoke (CS), both actively and passively through secondhand exposures, are at higher risk for respiratory infections, mechanisms driving this susceptibility remain largely unknown and may result from smoke-induced deficits of CC16. METHODS: In the current study, we have begun investigating the downregulation of CC16 after acute secondhand CS exposure and its impact on secretion of antimicrobial and antiviral proteins. We cultured wild type (WT) and Cc16-/- murine tracheal epithelial cells (MTECs) on transwell membranes at an air-liquid interface. Differentiated MTECs were acutely exposed to CS or filtered air (FA) in a Teague TE-10B chamber. Apical and basolateral secretions were collected, and RNA was isolated for further analysis. RESULTS: After acute exposure to CS, WT MTECs initially responded by decreasing transcription of CC16 (Scgb1a1), SPLUNC1 (Bpifa1), lysozyme (Lyz2), lactotransferrin (Ltf), and surfactant protein D (Sftpd), while transcription of CYP1A1 (Cyp1a1), identified as being overexpressed in smokers and patients with COPD, was increased. However, by 24 hours post-exposure, transcription of these factors returned to baseline. Additionally, apical secretion of CC16 was initially decreased, but recovered by 24 hours. In all cases, the most dramatic differences were observed 12 hours post exposure. In our Cc16-/- MTECs, we observed even larger decreases in the transcription of the antimicrobials, but smaller increases in CYP1A1, compared to WT MTECs 12 hours post CS exposure. CONCLUSIONS: While most prior studies have focused on chronic CS exposure models to study the mechanisms leading to decreased respiratory epithelial CC16 expression, our studies indicate that acute CS exposure leads to transient decreases in expression of CC16 and antimicrobial proteins. These decreases may be responsible for increased susceptibility to infection.

abstract: Abstract Introduction: Valley Fever (VF) is a common cause of pneumonia in the southwest US caused by the fungus Coccidioides (Coxy). Diagnosis is often secured by EIA serology measuring anti-Coxy IgM and IgG antibodies in the blood. Antibodies typically disappear after a few months. We present a patient with VF who had persistent positive serology due to a cavitary nidus who required surgical resection for hemoptysis. We used a novel peptide cocktail to assay the T cell response during the course of disease. Case report: 56 year old with type 2 diabetes (Hgb A1c = 11.3) presented with cough and weight loss of 2 months duration. VF was diagnosed with a positive IgG EIA and CF (complement fixation) titer 1:16. The patient experienced initial improvement on fluconazole but was only intermittently adherent to therapy. Despite several months of fluconazole therapy, CF titers remained positive, and hemoptysis emerged. CT scan showed a cavitary lesion in the right lower lobe (RLL). Bronchoscopy was performed and confirmed RLL was the sole source of bleeding. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) showed 40% neutrophils and 13% lymphocytes. No pathogen grew on BAL culture. Hemoptysis persisted and 18 months after diagnosis the patient had an uncomplicated surgical resection of the cavity. Cultures were positive for Coccidioides posadasii, and latest (Hgb A1c = 9). Hemoptysis resolved following resection and the patient remains on fluconazole therapy 9 months after resection. Discussion: The majority of patients with VF are asymptomatic, have a mild course that resolves without therapy or a pneumonia syndrome that requires several months of therapy. Serology usually reverts to negative after a few months. In our patient persistent serology was indicative of an ongoing smoldering cavitary infection leading to the complication of hemoptysis. Cavitary Coxy occurs in approximately 10% of coxy pneumonia patients and resolves less frequently in patients with diabetes. To further elucidate the disease activity, we used a novel VF peptide cocktail which correlated with disease state. Our preliminary data suggests measurement of T cell activity may be another way to confirm infection or disease activity.

abstract: Abstract Description of the Case: A 65-year-old female with COPD, chronic hypoxemic respiratory failure, chronic heart failure with recovered ejection fraction, and untreated obstructive sleep apnea was admitted for progressive dyspnea and chest pain persisting for over two weeks. Notable findings on admission included an EKG showing right axis deviation with t-wave inversions in the anterolateral leads, negative troponins but also revealed an elevated protein gap which was first observed months earlier. Investigation for plasma cell dyscrasia was conducted alongside cardiac workup. Chest CT revealed chronic emphysematous changes with a moderate right pleural effusion and small pericardial effusion. Cardiac MRI was negative for inflammatory or infiltrative disease but revealed significantly reduced right-sided function with marked RV pressure and volume overload, which were new findings compared to an echocardiogram from a few months earlier. Subsequent RHC revealed PAP 80/50 (mean 59 mmHg), RAP 33/30, CO 4.11 L/min, CI 2.59 L/min/m2 and PVR 6.3 woods units, LVEDP was 15 mmHg. Overall, the RHC was consistent with a precapillary etiology of pulmonary hypertension. Simultaneous LHC noted unremarkable luminal irregularities in the coronary vessels. V/Q scan did not show evidence of a mismatched defect. Diagnosis of multiple myeloma was confirmed after bone marrow biopsy. Serum viscosity was within normal limits, but was collected after treatment initiation. Given the diagnosis of Group V pulmonary hypertension, she was started on diuretics in addition to PDE5 inhibitor and oral prostacyclin therapies which improved her symptoms dramatically. These therapies were continued for symptom management with the expectation of resolution with simultaneous treatment of the primary pathology of multiple myeloma. Discussion: Recent literature shows that patients with multiple myeloma develop pulmonary hypertension at greater rates than other common comorbidities, suggesting anywhere between 27% and 32% of patients newly diagnosed with multiple myeloma had pulmonary hypertension compared to only 3.6% of people with left heart disease, 0.7% with lung disease, and 1.4% with thromboembolic disease. While etiologies of pulmonary hypertension in multiple myeloma have been proposed, the pathophysiology is unknown. Overall, the diagnosis of Group V pulmonary hypertension in multiple myeloma requires clinical and radiologic indicators with evidence of hemodynamic changes on RHC. Panels A, B: Cardiac MRI showing a dilated right ventricle and right pleural effusion. Significant bowing of the right ventricle into the left ventricle is noted with evidence of septal displacement and septal hypertrophy. Panels C, D: Skeletal survey showing lytic lesions in the skull and proximal humerus.

abstract: Abstract Introduction: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a disaster disease characterized by obliterative vascular remodeling and persistent increase of vascular resistance, leading to right heart failure and premature death. Understanding the cellular and molecular mechanisms will help develop novel therapeutic approaches for PAH patients. Hypothesis: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis fosters better understanding of the cellular and molecular mechanisms that drive the initiation and progression of PAH. Methods: Flash-frozen lung tissues from 10 healthy donors, 10 idiopathic PAH, 10 drug and toxin induced PAH, 10 systemic and pulmonary shunting induced PAH patients of varying sexes, ethnicities and ages, were obtained from Pulmonary Hypertension Breakthrough Initiative (PHBI). Lung tissue specimens were processed for fixed scRNA-seq. The cell proportion change, gene expression, and pathway analysis were evaluated between different disease subclasses, sexes, ages in different cell types. Results: Our analysis reveals 317,414 cells, 33 clusters and 9 major cell types, including endothelial cell (EC), alveolar cell, fibroblast, smooth muscle cell (SMC), pericyte, myeloid cell, lymphocyte, airway epithelial cell, platelet. Cell proportion analysis demonstrated an increase in the proportion of venous ECs, adventitial fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, alveolar macrophages, B cells, plasma cells and a decrease in capillary ECs 2 and pericytes in PAH lungs. KEGG Pathway analysis showed that upregulated pathways related to Herpes simplex virus 1 infection, ECM-receptor interaction, Complement and coagulation cascades, Hedgehog signaling and TGF-beta signaling pathway, while downregulated pathways enriched in IL-17 signaling, TNF signaling, MAPK signaling pathway in PAH patients. Female PAH patients exhibited an increased proportion of myofibroblasts, and platelets compared to male PAH patients. MsigDB Hallmark Pathway analysis showed that p53 pathway was upregulated, whereas inflammatory response, hypoxia, epithelial mesenchymal transition signaling pathways were downregulated in female PAH patients. PAH patients older than 21 years exhibited an increase in the cell proportion of platelets, SMCs, arterial ECs and venous ECs, and alveolar macrophages and a reduction of B cells and plasma cells. Conclusions: Our integrated analysis of human PAH lung atlas dataset provides a comprehensive illustration of lung cell populations and molecular signature in PAH patients within different sexes, ages and subclasses.

abstract: Abstract Background: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD), the chronic lung disease of prematurity, is characterized by sustained abnormalities of distal lung alveolar and vascular growth after preterm birth. We have previously shown that disruption of angiogenesis during critical periods of lung growth impairs alveolarization in experimental BPD and that lungTMEM100 expression, a proangiogenic factor, can be down-regulated in human BPD. Objective: To determine whether treatment withTMEM100 can improve lung vascular and alveolar development in a rat model of BPD due to antenatal inflammation. Methods: Time-dated pregnant rats underwent intra-amniotic injections with saline (Control; CTL) or Endotoxin (ETX) (10ug/sac) at E20, and the pups were delivered at E22 by c-section. For in vivo studies, lung endothelial-specific nanoparticles were used to deliver non-integrating TMEM100 plasmid by retroorbital injections in CTL and ETX rats at postnatal day 2 (P2) of life. At P14, rats were killed and lungs were inflated for histology and measurement of mean linear intercepts (MLI) to assess distal airspace structure. Hearts were dissected for measurement of Fulton's index to determine right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH). For in vivo studies, PECs were isolated from CTL or antenatally ETX-exposed rats shortly after birth using magnetic CD31 bead separation. PEC growth was determined by proliferation and tube formation assays with the following treatments: CTL (no treatment), TMEM100 plasmid (10ng/ml) andBMP9 (40ng/ml), a TMEM100 agonist. Results: After antenatal exposure to ETX, lungs from infant rats at D14 had increased MLI (p<0.05) and increased RVH (p<0.05) compared to CTL rats. Postnatal TMEM100 treatment decreased MLI (p<0.05) and prevented RVH (p<0.05) after in infant rats that had been exposed to antenatal ETX. Compared to CTL PECs, PECs from antenatally ETX-exposed PECs had decreased proliferation in vitro (p<0.05). TMEM100 or BMP9 treatment increased CTL PEC proliferation (p<0.05) and tube formation (p<0.05) compared to untreated CTL PECs. Similarly, TMEM100 and BMP9 increased growth (p<0.05 for both treatments) and tube formation (TMEM100 p<0.05; BMP9 p<0.01) for PECs harvested from lungs after antenatal exposure to ETX. Conclusion: We found that nanoparticle delivery of TMEM100 plasmid treatment after birth improved alveolarization and reduced RVH in an experimental model of BPD induced by antenatal ETX exposure. In vivo studies demonstrated that TMEM100 and BMP9 treatment increased growth and tube formation in PECs from lungs of control and ETX-exposed newborns. We speculate that enhancement of the TMEM100 signaling pathway may preserve angiogenesis and alveolarization, and provide a novel therapy for the prevention of BPD and PH.

abstract: Abstract Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a chronic, progressive disease without cure. Treatment can improve outcome, but informed predictions with clinical and genomic measurements can guide treatment and therapy choices. Previous research has focused on identifying clinical variables that could predict future outcomes. The current research aims to find genomic variants that can predict survival time. Whole genome sequencing was performed on stored samples from 325 PAH patients. We split samples into long survival and short survival using median, mean, and a strict definition where samples were included with Long survival greater than 7 years and Short survival with mortality less than 5. Variants were filtered for quality, assigned to genes, and filtered for function and population frequency. Genes are grouped based on Canonical Pathways defined in Ingenuity Pathway Analysis.Patients were 50% IPAH, 81% female, 97% european decent with a mean age of 54 at sample acquisition. Mean follow-up post sample acquisition was 5.4 years (range 0.6 to 9 years). For the strict definitions of long and short, mean long and short survival was 8.3 and 2.1 years, respectively. Of pathways containing more than one gene mutated in 3 or more samples, 31 pathways were associated with strict division of survival length using a fischer exact test. Bayesian network model generated for predicting Long or Short survival using the 31 identified pathways and has achieved high performance with AUC=0.75.An independent dataset curated by Triaxia was used for validation which provided 263 samples with a physician provided diagnosis of PAH and time to death survival data. Limiting to the same set of variants and using same long/short definitions, we identified 4 pathways associated with survival in the same direction (B cell Development, Cdc42 Signalling, Graft-versus-Host Disease signalling, and T Helper Cell Differentiation) possibly supporting the role that immune dysregulation plays a part in PAH pathogenesis. We identified pathways with biological relevance associated with a Long/Short survival time in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension with the intentions of using a group of pathways as a model for prediction of outcome.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Whether lung function in young to mid-adult life predicts premature mortality is unknown. Here, we aimed to identify lung function trajectories in the general population (age 25-50 years) and test their association with premature mortality. Methods: TESAOD is a longitudinal, population-based cohort initiated in 1972 in Tucson, Arizona, with extensive phenotypic, physiologic and molecular information collected at baseline and 12 follow-up surveys, completed approximately every two years. Vital status of participants was ascertained through multiple National Death Index searches up to January 1, 2021. We applied group-based trajectory modeling (GBTM) to identify patterns of lung function between 25-50 years using z-scores of FVC and FEV1/FVC, after stratification by sex and adjusting for age and height. Trajectories were also modeled for other risk factors: BMI, systolic and diastolic blood pressure (BP), pack-years, and serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Patterns of dyspnea (mMRC dyspnea scale) during this age interval were defined as never, inconsistent (<50% of surveys), and persistent (≥50% of surveys). CDC sex-specific life expectancies were used to assess premature mortality, with individuals who died before their sex-specific life expectancy classified as cases, and individuals who either survived beyond their life expectancy or were still alive as of January 1, 2021 were classified as controls. Risks for all-cause and cardiopulmonary (COPD or cardiovascular) mortality were determined using Cox proportional hazards regression, with lung function trajectories as the main predictor and age, sex, dyspnea patterns, as well as trajectories for BMI, BP, pack-years and CRP as covariates. Results: Simultaneous modeling of FVC and FEV1/FVC (N=1298) identified a reference (normal), a large FVC, and five suboptimal trajectories (mildly, moderately, and severely reduced FEV1/FVC [lowRATIO]; and mildly and severely reduced FVC with preserved FEV1/FVC [lowFVC]), each with associated probabilities of group membership. Suboptimal trajectories were characterized by deficits that were largely established by age 25. After adjusting for covariates, the severely lowFVC and severely lowRATIO trajectories were associated with the highest increase in premature all-cause mortality risk (Table). The moderately and severely lowRATIO trajectories exhibited the highest risk for premature mortality from COPD (combined adjHR=67.1, p=0.008), whereas the mildly and severely lowFVC had the highest risk for premature cardiovascular mortality (combined adjHR=5.6, p=0.004). Conclusions: GBTM identified seven distinct lung function trajectories between ages 25-50, with suboptimal patterns associated with increased risk of premature mortality from cardiopulmonary causes. This supports the relevance of early tracking of lung function as a metric for overall health.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: Over the past decade, vaping (e-cigarette usage) has taken over as a popular method of nicotine and tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) delivery, which has altered consumption patterns of tobacco and cannabis users. Current research on the effects of inhalant use to lower airways relies on cell differential data to determine the inhalant profiles of smokers. The objectives of this study were to measure longitudinal sputum cell differentials of existing e-cigarette, THC, and dual vapers via sputum induction, as well as to conduct transcriptomics (RNAseq) on the same, to assess for induction of progressive airway inflammation with continued e-cigarette vaping of nicotine and/or cannabis. Methods: Human subjects ages 18-35 were recruited, enrolled, underwent informed consent, and were categorized based on reported inhalant use: healthy controls, nicotine vapers, THC vapers, and dual use (both nicotine and THC). Sputum was induced using a 45 mL 0.9% saline solution via nebulizer for 2-minute intervals, for 12 minutes total, and were instructed to spit out saliva and cough after each interval. Collected sputum was treated with 10% Sputolysin at 37°C, washed, counted via trypan blue exclusion and light microscopy, and cytospun with Wright-Geimsa staining. Squamous epithelial cells, macrophages, neutrophils, lymphocytes, and eosinophils were counted by light microscopy and ImageJ. Graphing and analysis was done with GraphPad Prism. Results: Across our young, healthy inhalant cohort, induced sputum contained 51.0% macrophages, 44.4% neutrophils, 1.5% lymphocytes, and 3.1% eosinophils. Young, healthy dual vapers of nicotine and THC had higher sputum macrophages. Vapers of THC only had elevated sputum eosinophils. More abundant immune cells were observed in participants who continued inhalant use over 2nd and 3rd year study visits. Transcriptomics across inhalant use types led to the identification of 17 genes significantly increased in inhalant user sputum relative to healthy controls. Conclusion: Our sputum cell differential and RNAseq data suggest that young inhalant users have an altered inflammatory state within the airways. Further, our longitudinal data suggest that inflammatory changes and immunomodulation accumulate with continued inhalant use. Finally, more work is needed to tease apart the contributions of each inhalant in our multi-inhalant users. We are currently using nicotine and cannabis markers in the plasma and urine to re-categorize our inhalant users, to see if the findings based on self-report still hold.

abstract: Abstract Rationale: The 7th World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension highlighted the importance of patient-reported outcomes in clinical assessment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Patient-reported outcomes, such as health-related quality of life (HRQOL), have been associated with morbidity and mortality in PAH, but the added value of HRQOL measures to validated risk prediction models remains unknown. Methods: Adults with RHC-proven PAH from the Redefining Pulmonary Hypertension through Pulmonary Vascular Disease Phenomics (PVDOMICS) Study, a multi-center observational study, were included in this study. The Pulmonary Hypertension Association Registry (PHAR) was used as a validation cohort. HRQOL was measured using the emPHasis-10 score, where higher scores reflect worse HRQOL. Noninvasive risk assessment was measured by REVEAL Lite 2 risk score, categorized into 3-strata. Cox proportional hazard models were used to model survival evaluating the interaction between risk strata and HRQOL scores, adjusting for age, sex, and incident diagnosis. Harrell's C-statistics were calculated to compare discriminative performance. Results: From the PVDOMICS and PHAR cohorts, 265 and 2671 individuals with PAH and complete emPHasis-10 and REVEAL Lite 2 scores were included. Both cohorts had similar demographics, with an average age of 52±13 and 56±16 years, 75% and 72% female, 81% and 75% White, in the PVDOMICS and PHAR cohorts respectively. Over 87% of PVDOMICS were prevalent cases of PAH, while in the PHAR half were incident. Most individuals (62%) in PVDOMICS were REVEAL Lite 2 low risk, with 16% intermediate and 22% high risk; by contrast, in PHAR 33% were low, 29% intermediate, and 38% high risk. REVEAL Lite 2 scores demonstrated weak to moderate correlation with emPHasis-10 scores in both cohorts (PVDOMICS r=0.48 p<0.001; PHAR r=0.33 p<0.001). Notably, the full range of emPHasis-10 scores were observed in the low-risk individuals across both cohorts. In the PVDOMICS adjusted Cox models, higher emPHasis-10 scores predicted poorer survival (p=0.047) particularly among low-risk individuals (interaction versus high-risk group p=0.08). Similar adjusted models in PHAR demonstrated emPHasis-10 to be a confounder (p=0.001) without significant interaction by risk strata (low vs high-risk interaction p=0.94), but the greatest change in median survival time was observed in the low-risk group (Figure 1). Addition of emPHasis-10 to REVEAL Lite 2 scores improved discrimination in predicting survival (PVDOMICS: C-statistic 0.71 vs 0.73; PHAR: C-statistic 0.67 vs 0.69). Conclusions: Across two multicenter cohorts of incident and prevalent PAH, HRQOL as measured by the emPHasis-10 score improved discrimination for survival, particularly among individuals with lower risk scores.
